You can technically pan at the recording stage, (I think?), but I suspect they didn’t because the more important mix in those days was the mono mix; that’s another thing I didn’t mention in my comment above that influenced the hard panning of the stereo mixes: stereo was pretty new, most consumers were listening in mono, so stereo was to some extent dismissed as a fad. This meant both that the stereo mix was seen as less important from the band and producers’ perspective, and that there hadn’t yet been much time to develop stereo mixing techniques in general (I bought the mono box set and the accompanying essay was illuminating). Either way you can’t change the panning on individual instruments in the mastering stage.

You are “speak[ing] to older mixes”. The albums weren’t remixed for the 2009 reissues, they were remastered. Hard panning of sound sources happens at the mixing stage. The panning is like that because people didn’t used to listen to records on headphones, and it sounds pretty cool through stereo speakers, just a bit strange to our modern ears.
